solution:
**(A)** Elephantiasis

Elephantiasis is caused by the filarial worm *Wuchereria bancrofti*, whose larvae must develop inside a female *Culex* mosquito before they can infect a person, so blood carried on a needle cannot pass it on. AIDS and hepatitis B spread through shared needles, and the malarial parasite lives in red blood cells, so it too can be carried in blood by a shared needle or a transfusion.

[Note: the chapter names needle sharing for HIV and hepatitis B but does not discuss needle transmission of malaria or filariasis; standard biology gives blood-borne transmission for malaria and none for filariasis.]

**(C)** Heroin

The chapter describes heroin (smack) as diacetyl morphine, made by chemically modifying morphine, which is extracted from the latex of the poppy *Papaver somniferum*. That chemical change is what makes it an opium derivative. Codeine also comes from opium, but it is one of the alkaloids present naturally in the latex rather than a substance made from them. Caffeine comes from tea and coffee, and psilocybin is a hallucinogen from certain mushrooms.

[Note: the chapter does not mention codeine; standard biology lists it among the natural opium alkaloids.]

solution:
**(C)** caffeine

Caffeine is the alkaloid in tea (and coffee) that stimulates the central nervous system. Tannins give tea its astringent taste but are not stimulants, and cocaine and crack (a smokable form of cocaine) come from the coca plant, not tea.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology gives caffeine as the stimulant in tea.]

**(C)** Emphysema

Emphysema, the breakdown of the alveoli with shortness of breath, is caused by smoking and air pollution. Liver cirrhosis is caused by chronic alcohol use, pulmonary tuberculosis by the bacterium *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, and malaria by *Plasmodium*.

[Note: this chapter links smoking only to cancers of the mouth, lips and lungs; emphysema from smoking is given in the respiratory disorders table of the chapter on respiration and circulation, and in standard biology.]

**(A)** molecule that binds specifically to an antigen

An antibody is a Y-shaped glycoprotein (immunoglobulin) made by plasma cells, and its variable regions bind a particular antigen in a lock and key manner. It is not a cell at all, so it is neither a white blood cell nor a cellular component of blood, and it is made by plasma cells derived from B-lymphocytes, not by RBCs.

**(B)** interferons

Interferons are cytokines released by virus-infected cells (and certain white blood cells) that stimulate neighbouring cells to protect themselves from viral infection. Histamines are released in allergic and inflammatory reactions, pyrogens are substances that cause fever, and allergens are the antigens that trigger allergies.

**(D)** stem cells in bone marrow

Like other blood cells, lymphocytes arise from stem cells (haemocytoblasts), in the liver of the foetus and in the bone marrow of the adult. Some then mature into B-lymphocytes and others are differentiated in the thymus into T-lymphocytes, so the thymus is where T-cells mature, not where both kinds originate. Lymph nodes are where many mature lymphocytes stay.

As printed this question has two correct options: both chicken pox and pneumonia can be contracted by droplet infection.

The chapter says pneumonia spreads by direct contact and also via droplets released by an infected person. Chicken pox, caused by the varicella-zoster virus, is also spread by respiratory droplets as well as by contact with the blisters. Malaria needs the bite of a female *Anopheles* mosquito, and rabies is passed on by the bite of an infected animal, so neither spreads by droplets.

[Note: the chapter does not discuss chicken pox; standard biology gives droplet infection as one of its modes of spread.]

**(B)** Western blot

ELISA is used first to detect HIV antibodies, and the highly specific Western blot is then used as the confirmatory test to weed out false positives; it detects antibodies to the viral core protein and envelope glycoprotein. The Widal test diagnoses typhoid, and "Eastern blot" is not the confirmatory test for HIV.

**(A)** *W. bancrofti*

Lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis) is caused by filarial worms such as *Wuchereria bancrofti*, which settle in the lymphatic system and make the limbs swell like an elephant's legs. *P. vivax* causes malaria, a bedbug is an ectoparasite and not the cause, and the disease is only named after the elephant.

**(A)** phagocytes

Phagocytic cells, the microphages and macrophages, ingest and destroy invading microorganisms as part of the natural, nonspecific defence of the body, which is innate immunity. Antibodies, T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes belong to acquired (adaptive) immunity, which is specific and develops after contact with an antigen.
